utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I believe somebody has a housekeeping matter to raise. Mr. Milovancevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence wanted to raise an issue just briefly. As a Defence team, we have come to the very end. In addition to the cross-examination of the witness that we started examining on Friday, we have another two expert witnesses; in other words, we have been adhering to the deadlines stipulated by the Trial Chamber and we believe that things can come to an end as they have been planned. On Friday, the Defence received the text of the redacted findings of the military expert. The problem is that we do not recognise that. This is not our findings. We handed over something else and I really can't account for the mistake. I personally do not recognise these findings and I never asked for such findings from our military expert. The only way I can establish a link between the text that we received with our request is if I take into account the remarks that the Prosecution had to offer in keeping with Rule 94 bis. In that, what is typical of Rule 94 bis is that the Prosecutor can be of a position that some parts of the findings are not relevant, and this is understandable. However, if some parts of the findings are left in the text as being relevant, then this must have happened in very many places, and then the relevant places have been redacted in order to suit the Prosecutor's need. But in that case, we are going to end up with the findings that are nothing like the findings that we wanted to receive, and it makes it more similar to the findings provided to us by the Prosecutor. In other words, the Prosecutor engaged Mr. Theunens, a military expert, to provide them with their military findings that suited them and now they have another set of military findings that suit them, the findings that were obtained by our military expert. So, if at all possible, in order for us to draw our case to an end, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take this into consideration. The accused, according to the Statute, has the right to examine any expert in the same way as the experts are examined by the Prosecutor. What we have received is something that doesn't suit us at all. We would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take the situation in consideration in order to enable us to proceed with our work. This is the issue that I wanted to raise before we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what would you be asking the Trial Chamber to do? Just take it into consideration, nothing further? Because I want to know if there is a conclusion to your argument. Or are you just placing the matter before the Trial Chamber for consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for asking me this. The meaning of my intervention, of my address, to the Trial Chamber was to put forth a proposal. In order for you to understand what I'm talking about, it's this: The expert witness statements have four pages of the contents. The first part contains highlighted parts which have been redacted. What you see in front of you now, what has been highlighted, has all been deleted or redacted from the findings. This is page 3 and this is page 4. Everything has been deleted from page 4. In other words, in the text that we have received, there are 20 pages missing without any explanation whatsoever. Simply, pages 44 to 66 are missing. I have marked all that. I don't want to dwell upon that here in the courtroom. But I'm talking, as a matter of principle, that the Defence has the right to present their defence as they wish. If their defence case is weak, then the accused will suffer consequences; however, neither the Prosecutor, nor the Trial Chamber, for that matter, can impose it on the Defence, how they wish to present their defence. The document that we have received is a disaster. We do not recognise it. My proposal would be for the Trial Chamber to look at our findings and to allow us to present the findings, to bring the expert, the military expert, a General Staff officer, and to tell us about the topics that have been considered in the expert report. For example, an interesting thing here is the fact that when the expert report deals with the existence of paramilitary forces, whatever has to do with the enemy side rather than Mr. Martic has been deleted from the expert report. The paramilitaries are important; however, our learned friends seem to believe that when paramilitaries are mentioned in the context of the opposite side, then this doesn't have any merit. For example, when the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that Operation Flash is important and they leave it in the text, then the question imposes itself as to how come the whole paragraphs have been deleted from the text, and it seems that only the paragraphs that are of some importance for the Prosecution have been left in the text. But we can draw our conclusions only when we hear the military expert. The essence of my intervention is the fact that the text is not familiar either to the Prosecutor or to the Trial Chamber or to the Defence. This was done by an officer who spent 20 years working in the General Staff. We have invited him to talk to you and then you will be able to draw your conclusion, contrasting his words with everything else that you've heard. I raised this issue at the very beginning, Your Honour, only to give us time for the expert to prepare himself to come here and to present his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm a little concerned about the time, since I committed to finishing in two sessions and I've already lost some time from one of those two sessions, but it seems to me, as I understand Defence counsel, this is essentially an oral motion to reconsider the Trial Chamber's decision of Friday. It seems to me that that should be done in writing. And I can just say, from the oral motion, I've certainly heard nothing that would justify, in our view, a reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's findings. Certainly, we would reject the notion that what's been left unredacted is simply what's good for the Prosecution. I don't think that that's what's happened at all. Those were not what the -- those were not the grounds for our motion and I'm confident that that was not the basis of the decision. But, in any event, it seems to me that if the Defence wants to seek a reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's motion, or rather, decision, it should file a written motion to do so and we'll respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a brief remark, if I may. Obviously, we are going to issue a written response, but I'm trying to gain time and this is the only reason why I raised this issue. Any written submission has to be prepared, has to be sent to the Trial Chamber, which all takes time, and we are running out of time, unfortunately. What I wanted to say, in response to my learned friend's words, is this: The proposal for the expert witness's report is nothing else but a hostile attitude of the Prosecution towards the Defence. The Prosecution is in no position to decide how the accused is going to present his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I do think you do need to put your motion on paper if you want a reconsideration of the decision of the Chamber. From what you have said since you started talking, I have 101 questions to ask which, if I did ask, we will spend the whole of today talking about this thing. I think, in the interests of time, may I suggest that you make a proper filing of your motion, put your grounds of objection to the decision, and then let the Chamber deal with that. For now, I can say we have heard what you say; we bear that in mind. As you said, we must consider it. We are considering it. But to enable the Chamber to consider it properly, I think put it on paper and let's have a look at it. Thank you so much. May I just also mention that the decision that the Chamber handed down on Friday was oral and the Chamber did indicate that it will file a reasoned, written decision today, and it is being filed as we speak. Thank you very much. May we call the witness, Mr. Milovancevic, if you are done?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is actually my learned friend's time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I could note that I had an opportunity over the weekend to review that last exhibit. We have no objection to that being made an exhibit, the excerpt of the transcript, so if that could be given an exhibit number. I also note that I did lose 15 minutes, which I hope I won't need, but if I will, I will ask for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The excerpt of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: An excerpt of a transcript. It was at the very end of the session on Friday, and it's -- the ERN number is 01510096. I believe it -- at the end, the Defence counsel moved for it to be an exhibit. We asked for time to just look at it over the weekend, and I'm satisfied that it can be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I remember now. Thank you very much. That exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 1015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dobrijevic. Sorry we had to ask you to wait a little bit because there were some little things to attend to. Let me just remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Alex Whiting. I'm one of the prosecutors in the case and it's now my turn to ask you some questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to listen very carefully to my questions and limit your answers to just my questions, please, because we have to get through your cross-examination and we have limited time. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to first start with just a few basics that we may actually agree on. When you talk about Banija, the region of Banija, that includes the municipalities of Petrinja, Glina, Kostajnica, Dvor, and part of Sisak, which was, I believe, known as Sisak, Kaprag; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it is not Kaprag but Caprag.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than that, do you agree with what I said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you, yourself, lived in Sisak until the 15th of June, 1991, and from the 15th of June, 1991, until the beginning of August, you were in Belgrade; and then at the beginning of August 1991, you returned to Samarica; correct? Samarica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade and I took my family there. Actually, not to Belgrade but to Serbia proper, because my wife hails from Srem, which is part of Serbia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you focus, please, really, on the question. You went to Serbia, and that was on the 15th of June, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you returned to the Banija region at the beginning of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I returned to Sisak and I worked there for a few more days, and then on the 1st of August I went to Serbia and I did not return to Sisak but to Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. When did you return to Banija?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was on the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you, yourself, spent only a matter of days in Serbia; first in June and then in August.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And when you returned to Banija, you returned to Samarica; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Samarica is located in the Dvor municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Partly in Dvor and partly in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified that when you returned to Samarica in August of 1991, your task was to organise the Territorial Defence in the Serbian villages of Sisak, Caprag, that were part of the SAO Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to organise it. I already found some sort of organisation there. There was a mini staff in the village of Mala Gradusa and there were a few -- hundreds of people there who had already organised themselves and who already had village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Your function, then, was you were a deputy or an assistant in the staff of that TO, of Sisak, Caprag; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the municipality of Sisak, Caprag, borders on Kostajnica, and so when you talk about events that occurred in Kostajnica in 1991, it is because, as you say - and now I'm quoting you from Friday, at page 10887 - that you were "in the immediate vicinity in all these actions and operations that were unfolding"; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some individuals were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Now, you assumed a function that related to the entire area of Banija only at the end of 1992, in December of 1992, when you became a coordinator for the SUP of Banija. And you held that position for some period of months, until, I believe, April of 1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to be very clear with you, so I'm going to put to you what our position is from the very beginning, and it's also because I may not be able to put to you all of the evidence related to these issues. I want to put to you that with respect to 1991, either you do not know what was happening in the entire area of Banija or you are choosing not to tell the Trial Chamber, because what you have testified about what was happening in Banija does not correspond to reality. The reality is that the police of the SAO Krajina, both special units and the regular police, were operating all over the region of Banija, starting from at least June of 1991, and they were operating in all of the areas seized by Serbs from then, the summer of 1991, through 1991 and into 1992, and these police were under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina. Do you understand our position, and do you agree with it? And you can answer that yes or no. There are two questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a pop quiz and I don't feel that I should be answering by just yes or no. You've asked me something that requires a broad answer from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let me explain. I understand why you might be inclined to think that. I'm going to go through these points in some detail and ask you specific questions. I just wanted to give you our overall position from the very start. So my question is: Do you understand our position, and do you agree with it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying but I absolutely do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can go into some detail about it. You testified on Friday - and it's at page 10897, and it was also in the summary of the evidence that the Defence provided to us about what you were going to testify about - that essentially the police began functioning in Banija, in the area of Banija, only in January of 1992. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we only spoke about the area of Kostajnica, i.e., the Banija triangle, where the Croatian paramilitary had taken Kostajnica. I said that, at the time when Kostajnica was being taken and then when it was being liberated, that in that area, at that time, the police did not function. I did not claim that for Glina or for Petrinja, because we did not deal with those two areas at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just actually read to you from what you said, and perhaps now you're changing your testimony. But the question -- it's at 10897. The question that was put to you on Friday was: "When was SAO Krajina Police established, and this time in terms of its being fully fledged?" Your answer was: "At the beginning of 1992, Kostajnica, in January, then Gradusa, Petrinja, Glina. This is the period when Krajina Police started functioning." Now, that's what you said, sir, on Friday. Do you now want to change that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. I don't intend to change my statement. It is an indisputable fact that in Glina the police were all the time the police that had remained there when the SAO Krajina separated from Croatia, and the same went for Petrinja. I was talking about Caprag, about the 23 villages that did not have any police stations at all. And I also spoke about Kostajnica, which, during the Croatian paramilitary occupation and after the liberation, I told you that Petar Vuruna was appointed in January 1992 as the chief of police in Kostajnica. And these are all indisputable facts and I adhere by all these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm sorry, because I'm still not understanding, because on Friday, you said that it was in the beginning of January 1992 that the Kostajnica Police started, and you said also it was then that the police, the Krajina Police, was formed in Petrinja and Glina. Now, that's what you said on Friday. Are you now saying that, in fact, the SAO Krajina Police operated in Petrinja and Glina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak about the SAO Krajina Police. I was talking about the police station that remained in Petrinja and in Glina. Those were police stations which never discontinued their work. Those police stations continuously worked --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you and see if I can get clarity on this. What is your -- on Friday, certainly with that answer, you stated that the SAO Krajina Police was not established in Petrinja and Glina until January of 1992, or even after. Now, today, what is your position? Was the SAO Krajina -- forget about the police station. Was the SAO Krajina Police in control or operating in Glina and Petrinja during 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't operate. I don't know how you mean "operate." Please don't forget that both Petrinja and Glina were under the occupation of the Croatian paramilitaries for a while, and that Petrinja and Glina were being liberated at the same time. While Petrinja and Glina were under the occupation of the Croatian paramilitary forces, obviously, the police could not operate in the way that they should have, under normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, how about when Glina was liberated in July of 1991? Was the SAO Krajina Police functioning then or not, in Glina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say the SAO Krajina Police, I believe that you're trying to say that this was a single linked-up service of the interior that functioned across the entire territory. But this simply wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm afraid I'm going to interrupt you. My question was very specific. I was asking you about Glina in July of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glina, in 1991, was liberated and it was liberated by the army, by the unit under the command of Colonel Boric. This was the unit that liberated Glina. And then after that, in Glina, the police remained and continued operating in the territory of the municipality of Glina. Later on the linking up --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please, really listen -- I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- you can understand my questions. Please listen very carefully to my questions and just focus on my questions. The police that you're talking about in Glina was the SAO Krajina Police under the control of the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know whether you are the advocate of Croatia here or you're representing the international tribunal. What I'm trying to say is that the SAO Krajina Police represented the police of a state, and we are now talking about one segment, about a police station in Glina, which functioned in one way or another and was in one way or another linked up with Knin, or maybe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to intervene here. It's not for you to make that statement you've just made. It's highly irresponsible of you to say the Prosecutor is here an advocate for Croatia. You know exactly what position he holds here and he's asking you questions. Yours is to answer his questions and not to query why he asks you the questions. Do we understand each other, sir? You're not going to come --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you're not coming here to come and make political statements for your constituency back home, okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, how about Dvor? Was the SAO Krajina Police operating in Dvor after, say, June or July of 1991, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to reply to Mr. Prosecutor in the following way: Again, you keep talking about the SAO Krajina Police, yet what I'm trying to tell you is that those municipalities had their own separate police stations, and, as far as I know, at that time, they performed certain functions only within their territory. This is what I'm trying to tell you. As far as I know, the SAO Krajina Police, as a single, organised force, so to speak, began functioning only later on, on the orders issued from Knin and so on. It was not easy, in the early days of war, to link up all those police stations and to even establish police stations and then to proceed so quickly. We would have been a very strong and very large state had we been able to organise our government in the way that you're trying to now put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is your testimony now, sir, that there were police in these areas but they were not under the command of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina? They were autonomous units operating on their own? And it was this way until January of 1992? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less we can agree on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are only agreeing that that is your testimony, just so we are clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at Exhibit 183, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, I'm going to put it to you that, starting from January of 1991, the police stations of Glina, Dvor, Kostajnica, were under the command of the SAO Krajina. This is a document dated the 5th of January, 1991. It's from the SAO Krajina Executive Committee. And if you look, it's an announcement of the setting up of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina, Secretariat of the Interior. And if you look down, it says in that first paragraph, it says: "The Secretariat will include the police stations," and it lists a number of police stations, including Glina, Kostajnica and Dvor. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it says that, but I have to distance myself from this in a way. I personally did not have any role --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to take this one step at a time. Look at the first paragraph. It says -- if you could just read the first paragraph, it says: "The Secretariat will include the police stations," and it lists a number of towns and villages, and it includes Dvor, Glina and Kostajnica. Do you see that, sir? This is in January of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's how it was, wasn't it? Those police stations, from the very beginning, were under the control of the SAO Krajina. At that time it was the Secretariat of the Interior, and in May of 1991 it became the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, once again, that at that time -- now I'm talking about my personal knowledge of how the police functioned in Banija. I was not aware of these orders at the time, and, in fact, this is the first time I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, now that you've seen this order, do you want to change your -- is it now the case -- now do you say that you don't know, really, how the police was organised in the area of Banija during 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, and on the basis of my knowledge, I still assert that this was not any kind of a serious organisation and this was not a single force that was able to function fully and properly in the entire territory. I'm, in particular, now referring to the municipality of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, isn't -- you didn't know about this order from the very beginning of 1991, so you told us that you didn't -- you weren't aware of this order. So isn't it the case that, really, you don't know how the police was organised? You may have thought something but, in fact, you don't really know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely everything that I have said is something that I am ready to repeat. In light of this order, even in light of this order, I can say that at that time the police did not have even a theoretical chance to function properly as a single force in the entire territory. These were probably just some attempts to establish this single chain of command, but I can state with certainty that this was not established at the time, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, now you're saying that "these were probably" something. You're just speculating now what this order means and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question. I don't know what you mean when you say that I'm speculating. I have come here, I travelled 2.000 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in your last answer, you started to try to explain this order, which you told us you'd never seen before, were not aware of, by saying, "These were probably just some attempts to establish a single chain of command." But that's just speculation on your part. The simple fact is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I do know how the police stations functioned at the time on the ground in Banija, the area that I'm familiar with, and everything that I said about those police stations holds true. You do not have a single fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, the fact is you were a member of the TO of one municipality, the Sisak, Caprag, municipality, and you were never a member of the police during 1991. So how is it that you can be certain about how the police functioned on the ground in the entire Banija area, which is five or six municipalities? How can you be certain of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm certain because I travelled to Glina every day. That was the only place from which we got our supplies; I'm referring to fuel and other necessities that we needed to survive and subsist on the ground. So every day I would travel to Glina and to Kostajnica, and even before Kostajnica was occupied by the Croatian forces and after it was liberated, I was there quite often, so we had joint activities. In fact, we were a single enclave in -- we were encircled and this is how we functioned. So you cannot tell me that I was not familiar with the situation in Glina, Petrinja, Sisak, and Dvor. So you cannot claim that I was not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, do you have a problem with your earphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you just holding it? It's not because it's falling off from your head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was a comfortable position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's a comfortable position, please go ahead and keep the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But it's true, isn't it, that you had no function in the SAO Krajina Police or in any police during 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you offered the Trial Chamber your judgement about the police in the Banija area, you were not aware of this order which is before you on the screen. You didn't know about that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, you mean you didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another document. It's Exhibit 568. While it's coming up, this is a report from the Dvor Krajina -- oh, you're getting your glasses.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's just my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You'll need them for this document. It's actually kind of hard to read in the B/C/S, I'm afraid. And if it would be easier, I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I printed out a hard copy because I thought it might be easier, and I'll sort of leave it to the witness to decide if he prefers to look at the hard copy or the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report from the Dvor special police unit to the Ministry of the Interior, and it's a report on the activities from the 18th of June, 1991, to the 7th of April, 1992. That's on the first page. If you could turn to the second page, this report goes through the history of the Dvor special unit of the police. It says -- in the second paragraph, it says that on the 28th of May, a group of Serbian volunteers, headed by the author of this report, who is the unit commander, Simo Miletic, went to Knin for training and then returned from Knin on the 15th of June; and on the 18th of June, a training centre was set up in Samaricki Brdjani. In the third paragraph, he says: "The unit," in addition to training at the training centre, "the unit had also had the task of protecting the Serbian population in our municipality and wider, as we were the only organised armed formation in Banija and Kordun." And then I would ask you, sir, please, to turn to page 2 of the B/C/S; we'll stay on page 1, this first page in the English, and you'll see it's the third paragraph on page 2 in the B/C/S, and it's the fourth paragraph from the bottom. It says that the training centre was moved to Samarica on the 3rd of July, 1991. And then it goes through here -- and I won't go through it all, but it goes through all the different armed -- all of the different armed confrontations that the unit participated in during June and July and August of 1991. Do you see that, sir? Were you aware of these activities by the Dvor special police unit during that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of these activities because, as I have already said, at that time, I did not have any particular knowledge as to what each particular police station in each particular municipality was engaged in, what it was doing. In my examination-in-chief we, in fact, did not mention this area. It is an area with a majority Serb population. And, for all intents and purposes, the police functioned there the entire time. So I do not challenge this document because this is the first time that I see it, and I cannot give you any opinion on it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that answer, but just two or three minutes ago - it's at page 18 of our transcript from today - you said that -- you explained -- it's at the end of page 17 and the beginning of page 18. You explained how you travelled all over to Glina and Kostajnica, and then you said, "So you cannot tell me that I was not familiar with the situation in Glina, Petrinja, Sisak, and Dvor. So you cannot claim that I was not familiar." But now you just told us that you, in fact, weren't familiar.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really like to appeal to you, in the interests of the truth and because of the importance of this Tribunal. What I'm saying is something that I -- I am fully behind what I say. I said that I was not familiar with all the details of the functioning of the police. What I said was that I knew that there was a police station in Dvor, that this was a police station that never stopped functioning from the moment of the inception of the SAO Krajina, and now, as to how it functioned and all those details, this is not something that I can either confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now that you see this information about this fighting that occurred in June and July and August of 1991, would that now cause you to change your answer that the conflict -- the answer that you gave on Friday, which is that the conflict in Banija began on the 21st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to set a date. I don't know whether anyone has the right answer to when the real conflict broke out, when the war broke out, because we had known about some liquidations that had happened in Sisak a long time before we actually became organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was you who told us on Friday that you thought the conflict began on the 21st of August, 1991, in Banija. So my question is: Seeing this, does that change your opinion that you offered on Friday? Would you now say that, in fact, the conflict -- the fighting, the armed conflict, in Banija started long before August 21st, 1991, that there was fighting going on in June and July of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some liquidations in 1990, but what I'm trying to say is that the war, according to me, began when the roadblocks were set up and when the demarcation line was established. Before that, according to me, in the entire Banija --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Roadblocks were set up long before August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How would the Croatian police officers be able to enter Kostajnica and to slaughter all those Serbs in Brdjani, Cakale, and the other villages there? Had there been roadblocks there, they would not have been able to get in at all. So what you're saying now is simply -- it doesn't hold water. The roadblocks were put up only --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you could focus your attention on this document and look, please, now at page 1 of the document. In the fifth paragraph, it says: "On the 24th of June, 1991, due to penetration by Ustasha forces from the direction of Kostajnica, a barricade was set up in Dvor." The next paragraph talks about a barricade in Zirovac, set up on the 25th of June, 1991, and so on and so on. Would you agree, sir, that barricades, in fact, were set up before the 21st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I partly agree that in some villages the roadblocks had been set up, but I'm talking about the roadblocks that were set up, in my opinion, along the entire demarcation line, when it was no longer possible to enter the territory of the SAO Krajina because of the roadblocks. And, of course, it is true that in some villages roadblocks were set up. This was the decision of the people who were in charge of the Territorial Defence in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a different topic. Staying with this document, if you could look at page 4 of the document, and when I say "page 4," I think it's page 4 of the written -- no, just page 4, the fourth page of the document, and if we could look at page 3, please. And there is a paragraph -- on the B/C/S, it's the third paragraph down; in the English, it's halfway down. It begins, "On the 8th of September 1991, following a request from the Kostajnica TO, I sent --"

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I can't -- I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Look for a paragraph that begins -- do you see it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just read the next two paragraphs, please, the first one about the 8th of September, 1991, and the second paragraph about the 13th of September, 1991. It's about this special unit of the Dvor police participating in fighting in Kostajnica; right at the time of the liberation of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't assist you with this document because this is the first time that I see it. I don't know just how authentic it is, in fact, but I maintain that when Kostajnica was liberated, it was liberated by the Territorial Defence of Kostajnica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the participation of this special police unit of Dvor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that from the direction of Dvor, along the Una River, because there had been some fighting up there, that a unit from Dvor had been active here. But, in my opinion, it was not the key, the decisive factor, in the liberation of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware, sir -- and I'm done with that document. Are you aware, sir, that the Dvor -- this refers to the Dvor special police unit. There was also a Dvor public security station. Are you aware that police from the public security station of Dvor participated in fighting in Kostajnica, Glina, Petrinja, Dubica, and other places?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a reference to Exhibit 599, Your Honours. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that, sir, at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not aware of the fact that this unit had been engaged in all those fronts. This is not something that I know or have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know that on the 10th -- around the 10th of July, 1991, there were Martic's Police present in the village of Cukur, which is just west of Kostajnica? It's very close, maybe no more than a couple of kilometres west of Kostajnica. Did you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Cukur?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Probably. If that's a village that's just west of Kostajnica, then that's the village I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first like to ask you, sir, to explain to me what is Martic's Police? Why are you referring to this as Martic's Police? Is this the way that you call the police force in any country of the world? Do you always refer to it by referring to it with the president's name? What do you mean when you say "Martic's Police"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sometimes I do, but in this case I'm using that term because I'm referring to a specific document, and I'll show you the document in a moment. But for the purposes of the question, let's say "Martic's Police" is police under Milan Martic's command. Were you aware that there were police under Milan Martic's command in Cukur, just next to Kostajnica, in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know about that, but I must insist, once again, that Cukur was the first village --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about the village of Zamlaca, Zamlaca, which is in Dvor? Did you know that there was police under Milan Martic's command there in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Milan Martic would be the best person to tell you whether it was under his command or not. But it is my assertion that the entire area along the River Una, Zamlaca, Kozibrod, and then some other places, that these were all major and terrible strongholds of the Croatian paramilitaries at the time. And I know that there was heavy fighting there to liberate this corridor along the River Una, from Kostajnica towards Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're not aware of police under Milan Martic's command in that village of Zamlaca. You didn't know about that in July of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at Exhibit 01228713.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you see this is a document, this is a -- this is a document from the 5th Corps of the JNA, which is also known as the Banja Luka Corps, dated the 10th of July, 1991, and it is about -- it's from the intelligence department and it's about -- it's primarily about the deployment and activities of the Croatian police units. I'm going to ask that we turn to the second page of the document. If we could scroll down, you'll see the third paragraph from the bottom says that "Marticevci," meaning Martic's Police, "have blocked the bridge and mined it in the village of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Martic's Police is not something that is mentioned in the text at all. I would kindly like to ask my learned colleague to read exactly what it says and to show where Martic's -- the term "Martic's Police" is used. We have heard that "Marticevci" is a colloquial term, and, in fact, the witness himself queried the use of this term just now. It says here that the bridge was blocked by Marticevci, and these are supposed to be Serbs, I guess, because the other side are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It's true, it doesn't say "Martic's Police." I had misrecollected in the document. It says "Marticevci," which means Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In any event, the document says: "Marticevci have blocked the bridge and mined it in the village of Zamlaca," and then it goes on to talk about snipers. And then in the next paragraph, it says: "Marticevci are also billeted in the village of Cukur."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know why this cynicism. Perhaps I'm being too courageous to say that. But how is it possible for a man in Knin to be in command of every single person in this area? I have given you an exact testimony about all the groups that referred to themselves as Marticevci, or Martic's Police, yet they had nothing to do with Martic himself whatsoever. And I agree with Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. But, sir, here, it's not the group that's referring to it self as Marticevci, it's the JNA that's referring to these people as Marticevci.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who drafted this document and what were the motives for using this term or writing this. It would be similar to, if you were to call the soldiers who took photographs of themselves with the heads that had been cut off, for them to call -- for you to call them the police or the soldiers of the president of Germany. If this was the police, in fact, then there was a chain of command and Martic was the Minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, we are not here dealing with problems of Germany, okay? You wanted to know -- you said you don't know who drafted this thing. This thing is drafted by a person who calls himself Zdravko Djuric, Head of the Intelligence Department, a lieutenant-colonel. If you look at the bottom of that document, you will see that. Now, if you want to make comparisons with Germany, you can actually direct that comparison to this person who wrote this document. We are reading what is written there. It's written "Marticevci." That's how he wrote it in an official document from the JNA, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Having seen this document, sir, would you agree that, in fact, there were Marticevci in these two locations in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know what you mean by this term "Marticevci." Please, what is the meaning of "Marticevci"? Does it mean that if Martic was the Minister of the Interior of Krajina and the most reputable person in Krajina, then all people who were in war in Krajina bore the nickname "Marticevci"? I told you that there were so-called groups who called themselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please allow me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you. Is this the first time that you have heard the term "Marticevci"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. I did hear the term before, but I'm telling you that it is not appropriate to use it at an institution such as the international tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I have to deal with the evidence as it comes in. Now, if you could focus on my question, having seen this document, would you dispute that there were Marticevci, meaning Martic's men, in these two locations in July of 1991, or do you simply not know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, Mr. Prosecutor. I know everything about this. I'm familiar with Rastovac, Ustolica, Svinjica, which bordered on Mala Gradiska, where my staff was. I knew all the people who were there in these villages, who were waging war there. I'm really bothered by this paraphrase before the international tribunal. I'm bothered by the fact who defended Krajina, who were expelled in genocide, to call them Marticevci. Those were fighters of the SAO Krajina or something else. Why would they be Marticevci? This is not an appropriate term for these people, and I apologise for saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The term may or may not be appropriate. The term does not come from the international tribunal, the term comes from this document. This document is generated by what was then called the JNA. Now, you can't then erase that term from the whole document simply because you don't like it. It's not a term of the international tribunal, it's a term of this person who wrote this document here, who wrote this document in the name of the JNA. And we have to deal with the evidence as it is and get on. Please don't waste our time. Just answer the questions that are put to you and let's move on. Whether you are not happy about the use of the term or not, there is nothing we can do about it. It was written there by Djuric, and we can't erase it, okay? Let's get on with the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you please, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you please, sir, focus on my question. Having seen this document, do you dispute that there were - and I use the term because it's in the document - Marticevci in these two villages in July of 1991, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were fighters belonging to the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. Whether they were called Marticevci, whether they called themselves Marticevci, who called them Marticevci, I really wouldn't want to testify about that. You should call this Colonel Djuric to explain things to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just answer the question. If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were Marticevci's people -- Marticevci in those areas at that time? You can either say yes or no. If you don't agree, you can just say you don't agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just in the last paragraph, it says: "Following our estimations, the mood of the inhabitants of the village Rosulje, Slabinja, Zivaja, Rastovac," and so on "is positive towards the members of the JNA." So it's true that the JNA had been present in the village of Zivaja by July of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that it was Slavko Borovic's unit that was part of the Banja Luka Corps. We never disputed that, did we?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they were present there from July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the date. I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the content of the last paragraph has been misinterpreted. I have allowed for the witness to answer, but this is not good for the Trial Chamber. This is about the mood of the population towards the JNA, not of the presence of the JNA in some villages. It says here that there are some villages in which people display a favourable mood towards the JNA and some villages where that was not the case. It doesn't say here that the JNA was present in those villages. It just mentions the villages in which the population fosters positive feelings towards the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what has been misinterpreted? The statement that we read in English says: "Following our estimations, the mood of the inhabitants of the village Rosulje, Slabinja, Zivaja, Rastovac, Ustolica," and the other one, "is positive towards the members of the JNA." What's wrong with that statement? Just one sentence, Mr. Milovancevic. Go straight to what is wrong, because I don't understand when you make a long statement. What has been misinterpreted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the paragraph doesn't speak about the presence of the JNA units in those villages at all. It talks about the attitude and the mood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. I agree with you. It doesn't talk about the presence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 1016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, before you leave the document and it comes off the screen, I'd like to ask the witness a question. I'd like to ask you this question: It would be the second paragraph, a single line from the bottom of the page. "Marticevci are also billeted in the village of Cukur." What would you understand that to mean? What is the process of billeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the village of Cukur is on a hilltop above Kostajnica. It is a village from which you could easily control the entire area of the town. I'm not saying that in that area there were no units of the Territorial Defence. However, I could not accept, and I still cannot accept, that somebody called them Marticevci, because this is a term that should be discontinued once and forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I understood that evidence which you have given repeatedly perfectly, but what I'm asking you: What is -- firstly, let me get it in sequence. What do you understand the term "billeting" to mean? "Marticevci are also billeted ..." What is that process? What does it entail, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honour. On the outskirts of Kostajnica, there were Serb guards put up by the villages Cukur, Velesnja, Kozibrod, Komogovina, and so on and so forth. I already said on direct examination that our two lads were killed there - one was from that village and another one from the village of Velesnja - as they were keeping guard, so as to prevent units leaving Kostajnica and attacking the neighbouring villages that bordered on Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is it a formal process that is used in the command system or direction system?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: In the original text, it says only Martic's men are in the village of Cukur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that correction, because it would make a difference -- sorry, it does make a difference and I would then not press him. Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, in July of 1991, was the Territorial Defence in Kostajnica under the command of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, as far as I know. Not a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So this reference, in your mind, to Marticevci would not be a reference to members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't seem to be able to discard this document. Why do we trust this Zdravko Djuric who decided to call them that? Why are we talking about this? We had the police, we had the army, and we had the Territorial Defence, and it all depends on who was exactly where and at what time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please answer the questions and don't ask questions. Just answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would you not normally trust a lieutenant-colonel in the JNA? The head of intelligence department, would you normally not consider him reliable in reporting or making a statement in a document? No? Is it inconceivable that he could say something in the document that would not report the situation properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never said that, not for a moment. I only said that I don't know why he used this particular term. I never doubted a colonel of the JNA. However, the term, and why it is there, this is something that I find really intriguing, and this is what we have been arguing about for a while now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you then find a reference to the use -- to that term, "Marticevci," not to be a reference to the TO? That was the question that was put to you and which hasn't been answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't have enough wisdom to assume what somebody meant when they used the term "Marticevci." I don't know who he had in mind - the police, the Territorial Defence, the JNA. How should I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you don't know the answer to that question. The short and sweet answer is to say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take the break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I see your learned friend is on his feet. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to ask for five minutes before the end of the session for a very urgent matter that we would like to raise; maybe not more than three minutes. We would like to raise an issue that is very important for the rest of these proceedings, at the end of today's session, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the end of today's session, Mr. Milovancevic, or at the end of this session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had in mind was at the end of today's sitting. It doesn't have to be at the end of this session. My learned friend can continue without us actually wasting any more of his time. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting, you may proceed. Just bear in mind Mr. Milovancevic's request at five to seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I should be silenced by then. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that at the end of July of 1991, I believe on the 26th of July, there was an attack by Serb forces on the village of Struga?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that there was an attack. Units of the Croatian paramilitary forces were stationed there, and I said that this was a very important place for the transport from Kostajnica to Dvor. As far as I know, there were two strongholds and that there was -- what happened was these places were liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Attacked/liberated. They were "liberated" by Serb forces on the 26th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And members of the police participated in that operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, members of the police of Dvor Na Uni, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk now about Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to look, please, at Exhibit 583?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are done with the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's Exhibit 1016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a report from Glina, from Captain Dragan, on the 19th of July 1991. If we could go down to the bottom of the report, you can see that this is -- and this is on page 2 of the English. It is sent to the secretary of the SUP of the SAO Krajina, who was Milan Martic at the time, as well as the command of the SAO Krajina TO, Frenki, Major Fica, and a security officer. Now if we could go to the top, this is, as I said, a report - there, perfect - from Captain Dragan on this date. In the third paragraph, if we could scroll down a little bit -- well, it's actually -- in the B/C/S, it's the second paragraph; in the English, for some reason, it's the third paragraph. It says: "As for regular police and reserve forces, they all know their duties. The police carry on with their tasks as before." So, would you agree that in July of 1991, there were police of the SAO Krajina in Glina and that they were under the command of the SAO Krajina Secretary of the Interior or Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already stated that the police station in Glina, for all intents and purposes, existed throughout all this time. From the moment Krajina separated from Croatia, as far as I know it never stopped operating. The only issue is the area where it was active, because Glina was cut off from Kordun by the Croatian forces and Glina was also encircled. So one can talk about the control and the work of the police only in the specific area which was, by then, free from the Croatian paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you didn't answer the next part of the question. The police was under the command of the Secretariat of Krajina, as it states, of the secretary of -- Secretariat of the Interior of the SAO Krajina, as it states in this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the relevant time, I don't know what the link was between the ministry in Knin and certain local police stations, and how much contact they had. I can't be of assistance there because I don't know anything about those direct links and contacts, because I wasn't privy to the documents that you are presenting to me here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look at another document, Exhibit 582. This is a document -- this is another hard one to read, and I print -- I think it's probably possible to read it, but I printed it out, if you would like a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a document from the chief of the war staff in Dvor, Nikola Bojanic. It's a report dated the 23rd of July, 1991. It talks about a meeting that was held with Captain Dragan, the commander of the war staff in Dvor, and later joined by Milan Martic and representatives of the war staffs from Glina and Kostajnica. It says there was nobody from Petrinja. In the last paragraph, it says: "After the meeting was addressed by the Defence Minister," which in this document is a reference to Milan Martic, "and the staff commanders from Dvor, Glina and Kostajnica, Captain Dragan made an assessment of the situation in Banija, saying that unity had been established in the conduct of all operations in the area." Now, my first question to you, sir, is were you aware of this meeting that was held on the 23rd of July, 1991, with those participants?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would you agree with the conclusion of Captain Dragan that unity had been established in the conduct of all operations in the area of Banija? Or can you not comment on that or are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on this. I don't know that the role of Captain Dragan was so significant in Banija for him to be able to provide such estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, put aside Captain Dragan's role and focus, please, on the assessment that he made. Would you agree with that assessment that he made, that unity had been achieved in the conduct of all operations in the area, or would you disagree? Or do you not know? Are you unable to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would abstain from comment. I wasn't present. I'm not aware of the meeting. I see the document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. That was not the question, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree with the assessment that unity had been achieved in the conduct of all operations in the area of Banija, or would you disagree with that assessment? Or do you not know? Are you unable to answer -- do you not know enough information to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I believe that the text doesn't offer any basis for the question about Captain Dragan talking about the situation in Banija. When you look at the document, you see where the meeting was held, and Captain Dragan is talking about the situation in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to do this. I'm very sorry to interrupt, but I don't -- I don't -- there has been no objection and now I think we are about to hear some argument about the document, and I suggest that that's not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only read the last sentence of the text that is before you, but still, it won't be -- and I don't want to comment any further because of my colleague's words. This text is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't comment, then, Mr. Milovancevic. You say you don't want to comment. Let the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hereby my words, Your Honour: Anything else would be interpreted as leading the witness and I don't want to say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you focus your mind, please, on the question. The question is: Would you agree with -- I want to state it exactly how I put it. Would you agree with the assessment that unity had been achieved in the conduct of all operations in the area of Banija or would you disagree with that assessment? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would simply shy away from this document. I'm not aware of the meeting. I'm not in a position at this moment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must interrupt you, sir. Please concentrate on the question. The question is not about the meeting; the question is about the assessment made by the author of the document. Do you agree with that assessment, don't you agree with the, assessment, or don't you know, don't you have an opinion? Please let's concentrate on -- focus on the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I simply don't want to -- I don't have the right answer to this question that might satisfy the Trial Chamber. I don't know anything about this document. I don't know whether any unity was established at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you know what, if you don't know, say you don't know. You don't have to give an answer that satisfies the Trial Chamber. Give the answer that is according to your knowledge. Do you know -- do you agree with that assessment, don't you agree with the assessment, or don't you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've repeated several times that I don't have anything to say about this document because I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, not the document. The assessment made -- you're asked about one sentence. The sentence says that unity had been established in the conduct of all operations in the area of Banija. Do you agree with that assessment or don't you? According to your knowledge, is that fact or is that not fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer in the simple way, because I'm also aware of some other circumstances. In my view, what Captain Dragan stated is not a valid assessment. And if that is what is asked from me, I can talk about that. I cannot talk about the document because I'm not familiar with it. And I very much doubt that Captain Dragan was in a position to make any assessments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not asking you to assess Captain Dragan. We are asking to you assess a statement, sir. Just forget about the statement -- about the document. If it's put to you that Dragan has made an assessment that unity had been established in the area of Banija, do you agree with that statement or don't you agree with that statement? Forget about the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Why must it take so long just to answer a simple question like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the question wasn't simple, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was a very simple question. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you've actually now, I think, given two answers to the question, because at line 15 of page 40, you said, "I don't know whether any unity was established at the time," and now you have just said, "I don't agree" with the assessment. So can you clarify for me: Is it that you don't know whether unity was established or you disagree that unity was established?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that any unity was established. And I would now like to go back to the person who actually made this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is no need for that. Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic, which is events that occurred at Samarica, because you told us that in August of 1991, you, yourself, were at Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at Exhibit 567.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a report from the Samarica training centre on the 10th of August, 1991, when you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it says -- this talks about how the training centre was set up on the 18th of June, and then it moved on the 27th of June 1991. And it says in the second paragraph, it says: "The task of the training centre was to train special purposes police units of the SAO Krajina and Territorial Defence volunteer detachments to protect and defend people in the Banija area from the pro-fascist Croatian authorities." You would agree with that, wouldn't you, sir; that the purpose of the training centre at Samarica was to train special police units of the SAO Krajina and Territorial Defence volunteer detachments; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would agree partly. If we are talking about 200 people, then these cannot be both the Territorial Defence and the special units, because 200 people, that's a fairly small unit. That would be a two-companies-strong unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you this way, sir: Were special purpose police units of the SAO Krajina trained at Samarica at this time; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer. In order to train a special unit, the honourable Chamber is probably aware of this, it takes a long time. You need certain people who have certain prior knowledge. In this case, these were simply people who were organised in some way and trained to handle just the very basic weapons. So these were not any special units, because this was too short a time period to actually train such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's put aside whether the training was adequate or not. The fact is, special purpose police units of the SAO Krajina were being trained at Samarica at this time, exactly as is stated in this document; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samaricki Brdjani is actually a place on the outskirts of Samarica, on the road to Dvor, and as far as I know, Samarica actually covers tens of thousands of square metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We haven't got much time. Please listen to the questions and answer the questions that are put to you. You were not asked where Samaricki Brdjani is. You're just being asked whether special purpose police units of the SAO Krajina were being trained at Samarica as of the date of this letter, of this document. The answer is very simple: Yes, they were; no, they were not; I don't know. One of those three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm begging you, I really don't want to annoy the Tribunal. I don't want to say things that are not true. I was in Samarica where there is a hotel, where there are restaurants, and where the centre was, where people came together. This was used for cultural events before the war. And in the first days, in the early days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, sir. We are not talking about hotels and restaurants here, please. We are talking about the training of special purpose police units of the SAO Krajina in Samarica at a particular date. Do you know about that; and if you do know, do you agree or do you not agree that this happened? Please, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that there was a certain number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Do you also agree that at the same time Territorial Defence volunteer detachments were also being trained at that same place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about any volunteer detachments and I don't know about them being trained there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to -- oh, one other question about Samarica in August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a reference to Exhibit 508, Your Honours. I'm not going to go through it, but I will just put this one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Operational Group 1 of the JNA was based in Samarica as of August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
