utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move on to another topic. During fighting that occurred in Kostajnica and Glina in August of 1991, there were Croatian civilians who were driven from those areas into other areas of Croatia, for example, Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the early days, when the first incidents involving gunfire and the liquidation of civilians began, many Croats left their homesteads and went to Zagreb, to Sisak and to other places, but a large number of them remained in Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a document. It's 00290007. If we could look at page 2 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, unfortunately, I have this document only in English. It's a memo to Helsinki Watch related to an interview at the Red Cross in Zagreb on August 1st, 1991, and the memo itself is dated August 15th of 1991. I'll just read the first few sentences of it and see if you agree. It says: "Yesterday, all Kostajnica was evacuated. Some 2.500 fled to Bosnia and Bosanski Novi. One group turned and started toward Zagreb. There are 156 displaced from Kostajnica in Kutina. Some 400 got to Zagreb. We saw them in the plaza where they had a vigil and booth for collection of money for the displaced. The third part of this group went to Ivanic Grad, a suburb of Zagreb. Now there are 650 displaced people in Zagreb, mostly from Glina and Knin." Does that correspond to the information that you had at that time about displaced persons -- displaced persons, in this case, obviously, Croats, from Kostajnica and Glina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 1017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified on Friday that, based on the elections in 1993, you believe there were 1.200 Croats in Kostajnica in 1993. But in 1994, you'd agree with me that, according to the census -- I'm sorry, 1991, according to the 1991 census, there were 4.295 Croats in Kostajnica. So by 1993, approximately 75 per cent of the Croat population had left Kostajnica; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I spoke -- please, I spoke about 120 -- 1.200 that had the right to vote. Now you have to figure in all those people who were underage, who did not have the right to vote. So I agree that there were 4.000 Croats in Kostajnica before the war and I agree that about 1.200 of them had the right to vote. But I also said that 111 Croats participated in the Territorial Defence of Kostajnica, and they were the ones that took part in the liberation of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to get to that in a moment, but this figure of 1.200 people, that, you say, is the number of Croats who had the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But how was that determined that they -- how do you know that this number of people had the right to vote? Was that on some list of Croats who had the right to vote? Or what is that -- where does that number come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the number in the electoral rolls that was used at the last election before the war, when Racan won. The Croats voted in accordance with the electoral rolls. Serbs and Croats alike, in fact, voted in accordance with that. Not all of them took their right to vote, but there were 1.200 of them who had the right to vote, and a certain number of them voted, also, in 1993, for the elections into the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So that number, 1.200, actually comes from the election that was held in 1990, when Racan won; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Many more voters participated in that election. I'm talking about 1993, after Kostajnica was liberated, that over 1.200 Croats voted at that election in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, now you're saying something different. You said before that -- you said just a moment ago that 1.200 had the right to vote and a certain number of them voted, and now you're saying that 1.200 actually voted. Which is the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There has been a misunderstanding. In the examination-in-chief and now I'm saying the same thing: 1.200 Croats voted in the election. These are the Croats that had the right to vote. But what I'm saying is that the number of Croats that remained in the municipality of Kostajnica was much bigger because, of course, you had the entire families there with children, minors who did not have the right to vote. This is what I'm trying to say. It is not only 1.200 Croats that remained in Kostajnica but more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, even if that is true - and, for the moment, I'm not putting any position on that either way - but even if it's true that 1.200 Croats voted in 1993, you're aware, aren't you, that after 1991, the conflict in 1991, in the Serb areas, the Croats who remained were mostly elderly Croats, and the young people with families and the children, they all left. So even if this is true, this is probably the number of Croats that were remaining in the area, because the children were gone; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree with you fully, but it is true that a certain number of young people went over to the Croatian side to fight for that side. I would agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the figure of 111 Croat TO members participating in the attack on Kostajnica in September of 1991, that is just not true, is it, sir? By September of 1991, the TO forces of the SAO Krajina were staffed, virtually, entirely by Serbs, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, primarily by Serbs. But this information is correct. I checked it and those lists exist and can be submitted to the Tribunal. If you doubt, you can have the name, the place of origin, the date of birth, for each and every Croat that participated in the Territorial Defence and fought in the Kostajnica area. So this information is 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Where did this list come from that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every commander of a unit had a list of the fighters in the unit. Now, the Territorial Defence already had the squads, the platoons, the companies. We did keep the records. How else could we provide these people with weapons, with food, if we didn't have records on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But this list is, I take it, not a list that you prepared and not a list that you, yourself, checked. Because this is referring to the TO of Kostajnica and you were in the TO of -- I can't -- Caprag, the -- Sisak.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, not Sisak. Yes, Sisak, Caprag.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Forgive me. The list was not one that you prepared or you, yourself, checked; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked it before I came here to the Tribunal, and several times, because I didn't want to find myself in a situation where you would discover that anything that I told you, any fact, was not, in fact, true. So I went to the people in charge of security affairs there and I went, with them, through the information that I presented to you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But when you say you checked the list, what you mean is you looked at the list again but you did not, yourself, have an opportunity to confirm that those individuals on the list actually participated in the fighting in Kostajnica; correct? That's not something that you were in a position to do.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can't understand why you have this level of confidence in my evidence, when I say to you that this information is correct and when this information can be verified, if the Trial Chamber orders us to do so, through Mr. Milovancevic, in writing. So I have absolutely no reason to either enlarge or reduce the figure that I'm now putting here to you. You keep forgetting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you give the list to Mr. Milovancevic, or offer it to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I handed over to Mr. Milovancevic a list of 611 people who had been slaughtered in Sisak and he never asked me anything about that. So now I would like to ask you to ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not going to. I'm focused on this list that --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I am focused on this list of 111. Did you offer that list to Mr. Milovancevic? Did you tell him about it and tell him that that list existed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't cover this topic with Mr. Milovancevic at all, as far as I can remember. I thought that this list, with the 611 people who had been slaughtered, that this was much more relevant than the list of 111 people who participated in the struggle to liberate their own town. Perhaps this was a misjudgement on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir. Let's please -- I know you really want to talk about that list of 611 people. My questions about the 111 people. In the summary of the evidence that you were going to give that was provided by Defence, it talks about these 111 Croats who were supposedly members of the TO. So having heard that, do you now remember that, in fact, you did talk about that with Mr. Milovancevic, before your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that we actually discussed it, because I had a brief summary of my evidence. It's possible that it was mentioned, but I had no reason to think that you would question the validity of my statement, my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to another topic. You testified, and this is at 10888 of your testimony from Friday, that there were some "self-styled hooligans in Banija in 1991," but you explicitly wanted to stress that they had nothing to do with the legal authorities. Do you remember that testimony from Friday, sir, about the hooligans?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One of the two examples you gave was a group led by Stevo Borojevic, and you said that these groups were violent and would terrorise the population. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, Stevo Borojevic was a commander of a special unit in Kostajnica and was under Milan Martic's command in September of 1991; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look, please --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevo Borojevic was under nobody's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at document 600 in evidence in our case, please. This is a document to the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina on the 30th of September, 1991. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's a special police unit in Kostajnica, and let's -- if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, it's from Stevo Borojevic. If we could look now at the second paragraph of this document, it says: "This unit provides training to young people with its instructors who had undergone the training in Golubic. This is the only unit in this area that has remained under your command, while all other units have been taken over by the JNA and the TO." So, in fact, Mr. Borojevic, Stevo Borojevic, was in command of the special police unit in Kostajnica and he was under Milan Martic's command; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know Stevo Borojevic personally. He was at Samarica for a while. He was born in the village of Borojevici. He had his headquarters in the village of Komogovina, and that's where he gathered a number of -- well, 30, maybe 40 lads, who were a little bit -- not very well-behaved. And his deputy actually killed him. He was from Bosnia. And, in fact, they were under nobody's command. This is why they ended the way they did. They simply killed each other. They are all dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position that Stevo Borojevic was never under Milan Martic's command?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at Exhibit 601, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this is an order dated the 13th of January, 1992, from the Ministry of the Interior, and if we could scroll right down to the bottom, please, you'll see that it's from Milan Martic. It says -- it is an order from Milan Martic about the insignia of the SAO Krajina Police, and you'll see in the second paragraph there, it says: "Stevo Borojevic, Commander of the Unit for Special Purposes of the Kostajnica Municipal Assembly, is authorised to carry out/execute this order." Do you still say that Stevo Borojevic was not under Milan Martic's -- was never under Milan Martic's command?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, as far as I know, he was not under Milan Martic's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now that you see this document, would you agree with me that you don't really know what the situation was with Stevo Borojevic; correct? You don't really know whose command he was under.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether at the beginning, when this unit was established, whether he was really loyal to the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina, it is possible that it was so. I'm talking about the activities of this group after they moved to the village of Komogovina, when they set up their own headquarters, where they mistreated people, took away their weapons and did all this stuff that they actually did on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you'd agree with me, wouldn't you, from the previous document that in September as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way that my learned colleague is conducting his examination with regard to this document is designed to mislead the witness. The first paragraph is being skipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence counsel wants to ask about the first paragraph -- this document is in evidence. If he wants to ask about the first paragraph in re-direct, that's fine. I'm focussed on the fact that the command is given to Stevo Borojevic. That's my only interest in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any response, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document pertains to Martic's order to remove -- this is what it says in the document. It says here what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please respond to the objection -- to the answer by the opposite side. We know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, before the objection occurred, when you said, "Now, whether at the beginning, when this unit was established, whether he was really loyal to the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina, it is possible that it was so," you would agree with me, would you not, from the previous document, Exhibit 600, that in September of 1991, he was very loyal to Milan Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, are you referring to 601 or to 600?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To 600, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're not sure. You don't know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified about Milan Martic arriving to the area by helicopter. It's at 10890. Isn't it true, sir, that Milan Martic came by helicopter in November of 1991 to Zivaja, where the JNA was located, because the SAO Krajina Police in the area was in a dispute with the president of the Kostajnica municipality, Branko Mitrovic? And, in addition, the military police of the JNA in Zivaja, under Slobodan Borojevic, was seeking to establish control, so Milan Martic came because of that. And members of the SAO Krajina Police in the area were dismissed at that time as a result of those disputes. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I would object, Mr. Prosecutor. On several occasions, I've stated, and I still claim, that at the time when Kostajnica was liberated, there was no police station, and you are now repeating and insisting on the fact that the police existed there. No, it didn't, because all the police was part of the Territorial Defence. And it was a few days after the liberation of Kostajnica, as far as I know, it was then that Mr. Milan Martic, at the request of some people from the municipality and from the Territorial Defence, arrived in the area by helicopter and gave the authority to the army and Captain Borojevic to take over the bridge in Dubica that later on the Croats blew up, and that he gave them the authority to take over the entire power and to restore order in the area, because a lot of Croats had remained there and they were under the threat of liquidation from precisely such groups that had already started ill-treating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your memory is that this occurred a few days after the liberation of Kostajnica, which was on the 12th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But the document you looked at with Defence counsel, which is Exhibit 602, that pertains to Slobodan Borojevic taking over functions in the Dubica area is dated the 26th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I am mistaken about dates, but I'm certainly not mistaken about the event itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, you'd agree with me that it's just not possible that from the 12th of September, 1991, until the 26th of November, 1991, that there was no police functioning in the Serb-controlled areas of Dubica and Bacin, those areas; that those areas were without any SAO Krajina Police. That's just not possible, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to you. According to me, it is possible, because you keep forgetting that at the time Kostajnica was under the control of the Croatian forces and the Territorial Defence was headquartered in Velesnja, and all the police officers were part of the Territorial Defence. Where would that police have been in a city that was occupied, and what would they have been doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I think you'll agree with me that there was -- by September of 1991, the SAO Krajina Police existed in Dvor, in Glina, in Kostajnica, in all of those areas. Kostajnica and the area of Dubica and Bacin were liberated, to use your term, on the 12th of September, 1991. Are you saying that from the 12th of September, 1991, until the 26th of November, 1991, the SAO Krajina Police did not function in the areas -- in those areas of Kostajnica, Dubica, Bacin; that those were left completely without any police from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I'm saying. During that period of time, there was no police in the area and the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an area which you testified was very close to the front line, that was manned by the Territorial Defence. The JNA was present in Zivaja, which is some 15 kilometres from Dubica. You're saying, despite this military presence in this area, they let the area be completely uncontrolled by police? That's really your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying what I'm saying. I'm saying that in Kostajnica, the police was formed in January 1992, and that Petar Vuruna, the police officer from Zagreb, was appointed the chief of that police. That was the first police. I believe before him there was somebody else called Vujakovic, or I don't know. But this was only for a brief period of time, and then he went to Sas, because at the time a substation or a department of the police had been established in Sas, in order to control that remote area, in order to establish authorities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the truth is that the police of the SAO Krajina functioned in September, October, November, in Kostajnica, in Dubica, in Bacin, in all of that area controlled by Serb forces, and that in November of 1991, as a result of a dispute that occurred with the police, the SAO Krajina Police in Dubica, many of them were dismissed and thereafter replaced. That's, in fact, what happened, isn't it, sir? Or do you not know, since this was not actually your municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you were there, and I wasn't, then I suppose what you are saying is the truth. What I am telling you is my knowledge of something that I checked before I arrived here. If I was not sure about things, I asked people who were in the area at the time. I consulted some people prior to my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So, in fact, your testimony here today is not -- on Friday and today is not based on your own knowledge but based on information that you've gathered from others; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I will start getting angry. This is not what I said. I stand by what I said. Why are you putting words in my mouth? I simply told you that I adhere by my statement. Why are you going over the same grounds again and again? You keep on asking me questions that I've already answered. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please don't become angry. I really don't want you to become angry. I was just quoting back your own words, which you said: "If I was not sure about things, I asked people who were in the area at the time. I consulted some people prior to my arrival here." So isn't it, in fact, the case that your testimony here is based not just on your own information but information you've gathered from other people? Isn't that true? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir, I did, but please allow me. This happened -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've answered --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please, please, no. Your Honour, could I please answer? This happened -- please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened ten years ago. And this is what I knew ten years ago. And I appear before this Trial Chamber to tell the truth. Then I had to check what happened ten years ago. Are you trying to tell me that you know exactly what happened ten years ago without checking it? Why would I have any reason? I'm here to tell the truth. I have sworn to tell the truth. And please do not for a moment start thinking that I want to say something that did not really happen on the ground. And thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's precisely because these things happened ten years ago and you don't remember them all, that's why you went and checked with other people. Therefore, what you are telling this Tribunal today is not based on your knowledge only but it is based also on what you were told by other people. Is that not so? What is so difficult in just admitting to that? That's the question that you are being asked. Your testimony is based on both your knowledge and what you were told by other people. There is no need for you to get angry. The Prosecutor gets that from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic very briefly. You testified - this is at 10860 to 61 - that at the end of 1990, the Croatian police sought to move reserve police weapons from Petrinja to Sisak. The movement of the weapons was intercepted by the SDS and the weapons were brought back to Petrinja, and then the Croatian police conducted searches in order to locate these weapons which had been stolen by members of the SDS. Did I understand your testimony correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't. Those weapons that were intercepted were returned to the police station, and as far as I know, those weapons were returned completely to the police station. However, on the following day, the so-called police officers came from Zagreb, 300 of them, and they started searching houses with bayonets, with Kalashnikovs. They would pierce cushions. They started arresting people; a hundred people were arrested in Petrinja, and some of them spent as long as three months in various prisons. Those were honourable people, people who enjoyed reputation in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't, in fact, what happened that, after the weapons were returned to Petrinja, the police station was broken into and some of the weapons were stolen? Isn't that, in fact, what happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that some of the weapons were but very, very few. You're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the searches and the arrests that you described, the piercing of cushions and so forth, that was in relation to trying to locate those weapons that had been stolen; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only in relation with the weapons. This was done indiscriminately. The searches were done indiscriminately, from one house to another, and irrespective of the house and who was living in it, the same things happened in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified at page 10915 that, in 1991, "Croatian authorities wanted to turn the SDS into an extremist political party so as to be a counterweight of the then ruling Croatian extremist parties to provide justification for the then secessionists' endeavours of the Croatian leadership." Is that your testimony? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You quoted me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you saying there, then, that the SDS was, in fact, an extremist party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't. Not a chance. No. Please allow me. Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered the question and we have very limited time. So, in other words, this plan of the Croatian extremist parties to make the SDS extreme failed, in your view; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It failed; you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to ask you briefly about your testimony concerning what occurred on the 2nd of August, 1995. You testified that Milan Babic had a meeting with Peter Galbraith, the Ambassador to Croatia from the United States, from 8 to 11 at night, on the 2nd of August, 1995, and then Milan Babic came --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. That's what I said, and I hope that was interpreted. Milan Babic had the meeting, and then after the meeting was over, he came back and he recounted for you what must have been very dramatic words from Peter Galbraith. It must have been quite a dramatic moment; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you communicated through the night, so the night from August 2nd to August 3rd, with the delegation in Geneva and that it was agreed -- and they must have found these words quite dramatic as well, when they heard them; correct? When they heard those words from Peter Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it was agreed that whatever request was made would be accepted.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, though, on the 3rd of August, 1995 - and this is a reference to Exhibit 391, Your Honours - Mr. Stoltenberg reported from Geneva that -- so the following day, the 3rd of August, he reported that the RSK delegation in Geneva had not changed its position and had not received any new instructions. Can you explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with Mr. Stoltenberg's words. What I know is this: We received feedback information from our negotiators, and I told you who they were at that time. They told us that they had accepted all the conditions that were asked from them. The first one was to continue negotiations at Pleso the following Thursday, regarding the opening of the Lika railway, the political and military issues, and so on and so forth. This is what I learned during that night. And I believe that before me you had witnesses who were members of that delegation, and I don't see any thing in dispute here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. When you say you learned that during that night, which night are you talking about? The night from August 3rd to August 4th?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this was from August 2nd to August 3rd. In any case, this was on the eve of the attack against Krajina, the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at another document. It's 04179337.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document recounting a meeting that was held on the 26th of February, 1993, with some municipal leaders or representatives from Banija and Kordun and Milan -- Slobodan Milosevic and Nikola Sainovic. And if you see in the second paragraph, your name is mentioned from Caprag, Nikola Dobrijevic. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this statement that was issued?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read this statement. However, I'm familiar with the details of the organisation of this meeting, because I was in charge of all that. So whatever you want to know, I can provide you with quite a lot of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that the statement is issued in your name and other people's names? It says -- and if we can look at the last page, it's signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I take it -- I apologise, your name --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct. In the English translation it indicates that your signature is there, but we can see very well that you did not, in fact, sign it. So did you never read -- you never read this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the word "statement" there, I just want -- if you could just read those three paragraphs. You can read them to yourself. Is that an accurate account of what occurred at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very superficial account. I don't know who the author of this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we saw that it was signed by everybody but you. The question is not whether it's superficial or detailed; the question is, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly accurate, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you please identify what's not accurate. In those paragraphs, what's not accurate? If it's partly accurate, what is not accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please allow me, sir. This is a delegation from two regions talking to the president and the prime minister of a state. Would you please allow me to say a few words about all this. The meeting was initiated in order to improve the situation with the supply and the functioning of the municipalities in Banija and Kordun. The war was over. The UNPROFOR came. However, people did not have any means to live, and people, able-bodied men especially, started leaving the area. This is why we went to President Milosevic to ask for assistance from Serbia, economic or any other assistance, in order to improve the situation on ground. After that meeting, I went to Knin and I reported about the meeting to Mr. Milan Martic. I reported to him about the meeting in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for that. Can you tell us what is inaccurate about this document -- in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that putting an emphasis on smuggling, illegal trade, and so on and so forth. There were such things in every war. In this particular case, this was not such a strong fact in order to find its place in such a serious statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, is that statement inaccurate or is it just over-emphasised? You're saying "putting an emphasis." I don't know where the emphasis is put, because nothing is underlined, nothing is emphasised. Words are just written there. Now, just point to that which is inaccurate, not that which is over-emphasised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put it this way: This is all partially accurate, but the words that were used are not adequate, to put it this way. So everything is in accurate but not described in adequate words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, now you're saying two things. You said this is all partially accurate and then you say, "So everything is accurate but not described in adequate words." Just tell us, sir, which part -- just tell us the part that, according to you, is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I'm saying is that there has been an over-emphasis on the smuggling and on illegal trade. These things existed but they were not such a big problem. The economy, the organisation, and the way of life were more of a problem than smuggling and illegal trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, this document is accurate, all of it. All that you read is accurate, but it just doesn't talk about other things that you would have preferred were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So, then, don't describe it as inaccurate. We have taken 15 minutes' time to sort that little point out, when you knew that the document is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 1018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time, and I can assure Your Honours that I have about -- literally about three minutes more after the break, and then I'll be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We'll come back at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at Exhibit 1015, please. This is the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this was the transcript or the partial transcript of the -- if we could go to page 4 -- the fourth page in the excerpt in B/C/S and the fifth page in the English. This is that transcript of the meeting with Mr. Mesic and Mr. Tudjman and other people on the 12th of November 1991. Do you remember testifying about this, sir, on Friday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I would just like to read on from where you stopped with the Defence counsel. You stopped with this sentence, and see if you can locate it. I think if we scroll down just a little bit, it's about a third of the way on the English, and I'm not exactly -- I think it's now on the screen in the B/C/S, but I'm note sure. You stopped with this sentence -- it's Mr. Mesic talking, and he says: "Milosevic said that there is no inch of the land that he demands, which is supposed to be some kind of great Serbia, that he is interested only in the rights of Serbs in Croatia." Do you see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's where you stopped with Defence counsel. I just want to read the next three paragraphs, please, or next few sentences -- really, three sentences. Mr. Mesic says: "I told him --" and he is speaking to Mr. Andreotti there, or he's recounting his conversation with Mr. Andreotti, and he says: "I told him, 'Listen, sir, if you have been following Milosevic a bit, he was always talking, his mouth was full of Serbia and the rights of Serbs until a few months ago. If you follow what he is saying now, he only speaks of Yugoslavia and the continuance of Yugoslavia. In other words, he wishes to deceive you. He wants the Greater Serbia, but he talks about Yugoslavia, because now he would like to create Yugoslavia out of the remains. And why is the army at his side?'" And that's true, sir, isn't it, that Mr. Milosevic wanted the Greater Serbia but he talked about Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely untrue. And thank you very much for asking me this question. Had Mr. Milosevic wanted Greater Serbia, then, in 1991 and in 1992, we could have done whatever we wanted, so to speak, in Croatia, because you have to remember that at that time most of the army's assets had already withdrawn from Croatia; they were in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Territorial Defence had already at that time subordinated to the JNA. At that time we were already about to enter Sisak, Kozibrod, Karlovac, Gospic. We could have taken Sisak in four hours, flat, had this been what we had wanted, had it been the case that Serbia had attacked Croatia. We had a tank unit in Petrinja, the 17th Brigade in Gradusa, and at that time, Sisak was easy prey for them. This is just evidence that this was not about Greater Serbia; this was about keeping people alive, saving people's lives, saving and maintaining the rights of Serbs in their territories that they had historical claim to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in that last answer, you said: "... we could have done whatever we wanted, so to speak, in Croatia ..." Who is "we" in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now talking about the units that were stationed at the time when Croatia attacked the barracks and when the army pulled out of Croatia, mostly to the areas in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and about the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Krajina. At that time, in military and technical terms, we were much stronger than Croatia, and had it been in our interests to attack Croatia, we could have done that. And now we are talking about the state of Croatia that was founded on the genocide of the Serbian people. They expelled 600.000 people, Serbs, and this is why I'm bothered by the double standards being employed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to go down that road. Just one last question. Isn't it true that, by the end of 1991, Serb forces, including the -- in which I include the JNA, the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina, and the police, had taken control of all of the Serb areas in Croatia? And from that -- and from that, the RSK was born. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you are forgetting one fact: Before that, Serbs had been removed from the constitution. Before that, only cultural autonomy was sought, and Croats refused to accept any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, just before you start, let me mention to you that we must finish with this witness today and you must still have your five minutes with the Court, because tomorrow we are doing a videolink. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will now ask you some questions that relate to the cross-examination by the Prosecutor. Do you remember a document of the command of the 5th Corps of the 10th of July, 1991, mentioning the villages of Zamlaca, Struga, Cukur, Marticevci, that we talked about at length? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we bring this document to the screen - so this would be Exhibit 1016; could it be brought on the screen - could you please tell me, before that, who had the majority -- which ethnic group had the majority in the village of Kuljani mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a majority Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which ethnic group was in the majority in the village of Kozibrod, mentioned on page 2?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority was the Croatian population, and we had a very strong station there. Before the war, there was no police station there, yet when Croatia took those police measures, as they called them, against Banija, a strong police station, manned by several hundreds of MUP people, as called them, was located in Kozibrod, because that was precisely what they wanted. They wanted to cut off Banija's lines of supply from Bosnia and the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which ethnic group was in the majority in the village of Volinja?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was a mixed group, but Croats were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the village of Divusa? What was the majority population there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in Divusa it was half/half, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the village of Uncani?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uncani had the majority Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the village of Struga?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Struga was a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So when you say a Croatian village, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that it had a majority Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the villages of Struga and Cukur, which ethnic group had the majority?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cukur, it was the Serb population that was in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Zamlaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zamlaca, Croats were the majority, but there were Serbs there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at this document. Could we just scroll up a little bit so that we see the body of the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence, can you read it? It says that the intelligence department submits the available information about the deployment and activities of Croatian MUP units in order to update the working maps. Do you see this here in the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the text goes on to say that the bridge on the River Una, in Kostajnica, has been secured with two bunkers protected by sandbags. So now we are listing the Croatian MUP units and what they hold. The bridge on the Una River and the two bunkers protected by sandbags, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "An identical bunker has been set up in front of the Central Hotel." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where is this Central Hotel?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the Kostajnica area but on the very bank of the River Una, in the direction of Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So we have this following information about this Central Hotel: There is a light machine-gun emplacement at the belfry of the St. Anthony's church, with one observer and one sniper. Can you tell us, the church of St. Anthony, what religion is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the Roman Catholic Church, as you can see from the very name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, it says: "The gas station in Kostajnica has been seized from the Croatian MUP." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is all on page 1 of this document, in B/C/S. We are talking about document 1016. So we are moving on from the bunker in front of the Central Hotel and then the church of St. Anthony, and then I skipped two paragraphs and then we go to the gas station. So I'm just going from the beginning of the document downwards, to see what's listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't see the gas station, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's "filling station." It's the third line up from -- third paragraph up from the bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Thank you. I'm with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says: "The Djed elevation near Kostajnica has about 150 armed MUP personnel."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this elevation is located?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an elevation; this is a hill, in fact, which actually dominates the entire area of Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that, during our site visit, this is where we had lunch, in the wooden building on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says, as follows: "In Hrvatska Kostajnica, according to our assessment, there is about 300 Croatian MUP members stationed full time, about 60 members of the National Guards Corps, and about 400 reserve police. Most of them are billeted in the high school there." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this information tally with what you knew at the time to be true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are more people mentioned here than we assessed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it says: "In the village of Kuljani, all the yards along the road are fortified with sandbags." And whose village was it? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says further on: "In the village of Kozibrod, there are two bunkers about 150 metres from houses, family houses, and there are also some trenches there --" I would like to apologise to the interpreters. There, you also have dug in the trenches, communication routes, that are about 300 to 400 metres long. Kozibrod is ...?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then we have the next village. "At the exit from Kostajnica, in the direction of the village of Volinja, there are bunkers at about a distance of 250 to 300 metres." What did you say? Who inhabited Volinja?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said it was a Croatian village with some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "In the village of Divusa, the main collection point is the church, where there is an observation post and a machine-gun emplacement." Do you know what church is there, in the village of Divusa?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Croatian Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will not go through all this, but let me just put it to you that it says here that the field in the village of Uncani, that mines were laid there, signal and anti-personnel mines, and that there are two platoons of MUP and about 100 MUP personnel in the village of Struga, whereas there are some Marticevci mentioned in the village of Cukur. Do you see this in the document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this document correspond to the situation that you tried to paint to the Trial Chamber in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like us to look at a document. In my files I have it as Exhibit 600, and now I would like to ask my learned colleague Mr. Whiting whether this is the document mentioning Borojevic, Stevo Borojevic. I think this is what I have noted down, but I don't want to make a mistake. Can we now look at this document. This is Exhibit 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document? This is a document about Stevo Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the date here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 30th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now scroll up in this document to see the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the third paragraph. The drafter says: "We don't want to be under their command. We want to be directly under your command, where we have been so far." Do you see this part of the text?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So this person unequivocally states that he considers himself to be under Martic's command.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is his belief. This is what he considers to be the fact. And then he goes on to say: "Please do the following for us," and then four tasks: First, your direct command and tasks; second, legitimacy of the unit in writing; third, authorisation for operation and work; four, certain quantities of equipment, uniforms. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is, what is your interpretation of this information? You see a person here asking for authorisation for work, the legitimacy for his unit in writing, uniforms, yet he claims to be under Martic's command.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite interesting to see the previous passage. Unfortunately, you stopped taking care of us and we decided to present to you our problems in writing. This is precisely what I have been testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw that this document was dated the 30th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now leave this document aside. Let us now look at document 602. This is Exhibit 602.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not to waste time, this is an order from the Minister of the Interior of Krajina, Martic. This is the document that I showed you, Mr. Dobrijevic. Its date, the date of drafting, is the 26th of November, 1991. In this document, Mr. Martic orders, in paragraph 1, that "in accordance with the written and oral agreement with the commander of the Banja Luka Corps," now I will skip some parts, "General Uzelac. Establish authorities in wartime conditions in the area of Dubica, the municipality of Kostajnica, until a regular public security station/police station can be established in Dubica. All the tasks shall be performed by the public security station in Kostajnica, with the assistance of the Banja Luka Corps." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I showed you also paragraph 4 of this order, where it says that: "All people wearing camouflage uniforms who are not members of the SAO Krajina Police, who do not have appropriate authorised cards or have not been legally appointed in accordance with the appropriate decisions of the Minister of the Interior, are obliged to return their police insignia and to report to the military department in Kostajnica, in order to be assigned to wartime formations of the Yugoslav People's Army." Do you see this, Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is something that I had this little quarrel with Mr. Prosecutor about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see that Mr. Martic wrote this on the 26th of November, 1991; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the previous document, he received a letter from Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you about a document from January 1993 in which Martic orders Borojevic to act in accordance with the order --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It may have been interpretation. It's January 1992, that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is not misinterpretation. I made a mistake. It was in January 1992. Could you please provide me with the number of that document? I have two or three different numbers written down and I now don't know which one is the correct one, so could you please help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's 601.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is what I noted. Can we please now look at Exhibit 601.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that the Prosecutor showed you this document, dated 13 January 1993, containing an order. Could you please scroll down. The Prosecution -- the Prosecutor showed you the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the parties could be asked to make a pause between their questions and answers. If we do that, we won't be making mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the parties please make pauses in between your speeches so that the interpreters don't make a mistake. They have just made a mistake. They said January 1993 instead of January 1992. Thank you very much. Let the record show that the document is dated the 13th of January, 1992. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this first paragraph in this order in which Mr. Martic says as follows: "I order that all the insignia of the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina should be removed from the uniforms of the persons who do not belong to the police of Krajina, i.e., that uniforms be taken from the persons who do not belong to the legal military formations of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, i.e., the JNA." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but uniforms should be taken from those who do not belong to the police, and you said from those who do belong to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. I'm wearing a wrong pair of glasses, unfortunately. On the 26th of January -- November -- this is my question: On the 26th of November, 1991, Mr. Martic issued this order in order to remove the insignia and uniforms from all those who did not belong to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is not dated the 26th of November, 1991. It is dated the 13th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. It was my mistake. I was not precise. This is my question to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the document, in Exhibit 602, bearing the date the 26th of November, 1991, we just saw that Martic issued an order for the uniforms to be taken away from all those who wore them illegally. Do you remember that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Here, he sends such an order to Stevo Borojevic. Can you see that in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, what does he say about the order? Who should be copied?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report, pursuant to this order, should be sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, to be submitted by the commander of the unit for special purposes of the SAO Kostajnica within 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have seen all these documents, could you please share with us your position about Stevo Borojevic? Did your position change vis-a-vis what you have already told us?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that at the beginning Stevo Borojevic may have been one of those men who were loyal to the police and to the armed forces of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, but later on his behaviour, however, changed. He established his own independent unit and he did not accept anybody's command or control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In one of these documents, he, himself, Stevo Borojevic, says that he did not want the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, what was the relationship and attitude of Mr. Martic towards those who did not respect control?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted them to be disarmed and to be subordinated to the command of the JNA, or the Territorial Defence, which was also under the command of the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you about the presence of MUP units in the territory of Dubica, Bacin, Serbian Krajina, and Kostajnica, and that you were also asked whether the suffering of the population in the area had anything to do with their activities? Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at another document which is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would object. I didn't ask anything about -- I don't think I asked anything about the suffering of the population in that area, having to do with their activities. I focused my questions, I think, on the presence of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend is right and I will rephrase the question accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question by the Prosecutor was relative to the alleged presence of the MUP Krajina in Dubica, Bacin, Serbian Krajina and Kostajnica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Exhibit 290 from the exhibit list; page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the police administration of Sisak, Department for White Collar Crime, and it is about an interview with Josip Josipovic. The document has been admitted as Exhibit -- actually, as an official note which was drafted on the 1st of April, 1992. Can you see that in the heading of the document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 in B/C/S. I apologise to the Trial Chamber. This is a text that starts in B/C/S, on page 2, and this is in the middle of the second page, listing the names of some individuals. After that, there is a text that I want to show to the witness. This is how I would describe the part of the text that I want to show to the witness. It says here in the official note --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. This is -- objection on two grounds: First of all, this is about to be leading; secondly, this does not arise out of the cross. This is going to be about specific things that occurred in the area of Dubica and Bacin, according -- you know, and this document's comment on it, but I didn't talk about that, I didn't ask questions about that. And it's leading -- it's going to be leading to put this to him and ask him to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend has raised a number of issues that have to do with the control of MUP Krajina over this area. I want to show the witness a part of the document speaking about who has the control over the area. Nothing else. This is the essence of all the Prosecutor's questions: Who was it who was in control of the entire area? Was it -- on the 1st of April, 1992, the police administration of Sisak had information about that. And I'm going to put my questions to the witness so as not to lead him. I'm not going to put leading questions to my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's already leading to have -- it's too late. It's already leading. He has him read the thing and the answer is predictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend -- Your Honour, my learned friend doesn't know what I'm going to read or what I'm going to ask my witness. How can my learned friend know in advance why I'm showing the text to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are saying it's already leading, Mr. Whiting. In what respect? Can you just refer us to the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He said he wants to read the text that follows the four names, and he says he wants to -- and in the English, that's approximately -- just below the middle of the page on page 2. And then he says he wants to ask him about who had control in this region, a topic which -- in this region of Dubica, a topic which he did not address directly on his direct examination and could have. Having read this, it's already leading, because there is some comment about that here. So he's going to lead him into that answer by having him read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just read it myself. Mr. Milovancevic, it doesn't look like -- it does look like you're leading the witness, because the question that you said you wanted to put to him, you could put it to him without a document: Do you still stick by your evidence as to who controlled the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the purpose and the objective of my question is to establish why Mr. Martic arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you want to establish who controlled the area. Now, do you have a different purpose now from who controlled to the question why Mr. Martic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot avoid the establishment of that fact as well, but the goal of my question is to establish something that my learned friend has already asked the witness. The questions I'm referring to are about the circumstances that brought Mr. Martic to the area, by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll allow the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you part of the text. Momcilo Kovacevic is commander; Stevo Radjan is his deputy. "The control over the area is exercised by local Chetniks who are in conflict with Marticevci. Local Chetniks are responsible for the crimes committed over civilians for plunder, torching, and similar things, whereas the military police are trying to introduce peace and order. When Mile Martic came to the area in November 1991, he was in Zivaja, but he didn't dare come to Dubica. Later on, the military police did take over control. In the meantime, there were several shake-ups in power." I wanted to ask you this: Did you ever hear of Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radjan?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about Kovacevic and I did hear about Stevo Radjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention Stevo Radjan on examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know he was in control of the bridge in Dubica and I know that he was in charge of one of the renegade groups, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment. I'm wondering if we could be provided a cite from Defence counsel with respect to that last question, whether he mentioned Mr. Radjan in his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, will you please provide a cite as to where in the evidence of this witness he mentioned Mr. Radjan?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not marked it at the moment, but I know, 100 per cent, that the witness did mention that individual at the moment when he spoke about renegade groups and individuals. That was on examination-in-chief. He mentioned Radjan, and that was on the first day of my examination. I apologise, I don't have the indication of the page at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only him but also Mr. Japan, Stevo Borojevic, and some others, and I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can you do us the favour tomorrow to bring us the cite, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you also said, Mr. Milovancevic, that you wanted the witness to tell you why Mr. Martic had come, but you haven't asked him that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend intervened and objected. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you said you have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions about the control of the situation in the area and what happened. My last question was about the reason for which Mr. Martic came. That will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, can the witness tell us what, according to him, was the reason for which Mr. Martic came to the area by helicopter in November 1991, which was also recorded by the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that. As far as I can remember, on the examination-in-chief, I said that Slobodan Borojevic, who was the commander of the unit that was part of the Banja Luka Corps, wanted to leave the area because there was no authority, because there was no control, because of the wilful behaviour of the group that we mentioned. And the assemblymen in the municipality of Kostajnica, Mesinovic Glavas, and some others, had gone to Knin and asked Mr. Milan Martic to help. They asked him to come over there and help establish authorities and order there. I even answered to some additional questions by the honourable Judge Moloto about that subject, and I believe that we have elaborated that topic well and truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I have just two issues to raise with you; not questions, issues. You just said a few minutes ago that Mr. Martic did not want those who did not respect control to be disarmed and subordinated to the JNA and the Territorial Defence command.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said Stevo -- what's his surname?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Borojevic was one such person whom Mr. Martic wouldn't want because he was also disrespectful of control.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And yet by this order of the 31st of January, 1992, Mr. Martic instructs him to execute the disarming of those who are not respectful of control.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this question. I said that Stevo Borojevic and his unit, when they first had come to Samarica, as far as I know, he had been extremely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Let me interrupt you. We know what you have told us. I just want you to listen to my questions. You're telling us Mr. Martic did not want people who disrespect control; he wanted them subordinated to the JNA and the Territorial Defence. And I'm saying to you, on the 31st of January 1992, Mr. Martic orders him to do exactly that in his capacity as the commander of the special purposes police unit, not the TO, not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking for my opinion on this topic, I think this was the last attempt on the part of Mr. Martic to bring Stevo Borojevic and his group under the regular command, to bring them into the regular structure of the Territorial Defence or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't change the content of that order. You are changing the content of that order. That order is not trying to bring Stevo into any line.
