That order is saying to him, in his capacity as the commander of the police, special purposes police, he must execute the order to disarm those people who are disrespectful of control. Isn't that what that document says?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not how I understood this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you didn't, that's not how you understood that document, let's leave it at that point. Let me ask you the next question. Now, this question you may very well have answered; I may have forgotten. Where do you stay, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long have you been staying in Belgrade? Since when?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Operation Storm, the fall of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you ever go back to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have not gone back to Krajina, because as early as in 1992, I was indicted for war crimes in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are the records of what happened in the Krajina kept?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the records are not kept any place specific. Individuals, individual persons, hold some parts of it, and I, as a member of the Republic of Serbian Krajina government in exile, we actually hold most of the records that you're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say they are kept by individual people, I'm not quite sure I understand you. How do you know who is keeping what?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some important documents remained behind after Operation Storm and some presidents of municipalities, people employed in the administration, and so on, they managed to salvage some of the records and they keep it. This has not been organised yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please answer my question very directly. You said today, at page 49, lines 17 to 25: "I checked it before I came here to the Tribunal, and several times, because I didn't want to find myself in a situation where you would discover that anything that I told you, any fact, was not, in fact, true. So I went to the people in charge of security affairs there and I went with them, through the information, that I presented to you here." Who are the people in charge of security affairs there that you went to, and where is "there"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those people mostly live in Serbia, and I went to those people that I knew had security functions in the local units. So we are talking about people dealing with security affairs at the time when the Republic of Serbian Krajina existed and at the time when those units were legal units of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who specifically did you go to to check?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it is relevant to give you the names. I don't know how some of these people would react if I mentioned their names. If you think that this is important, I can perhaps do it in closed session. But I don't really think that these names are relevant. These would mostly be people who have these documents in their possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Relevance is determined by the Bench, okay? But if you say you don't -- you feel uncomfortable about giving the names, that's fine. You don't have to tell us the names. But relevance is determined by this Bench, not you. That is all. That concludes the questions by the Bench. Any questions arising, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Whiting:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that you're a member of the Republic of Serbian Krajina government in exile. What is your position in that government in exile?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a member of the cabinet. The government was set up in such a way that every region is represented by one representative who is then titled minister, and then he has his deputies. It would be a minister without a portfolio. I'm the deputy minister for Banija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who is the president of that government in exile?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president is Milorad Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic is still the President of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, as far as I know. The president of the government, the Prime Minister, that was Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down. Once again, thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you asked for five minutes. Shall we leave at 20 to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, since we don't have another witness and tomorrow we have the videolink testimony. I will not keep you long. The reason why I asked the permission to address you is the same as the military expert issue. Tomorrow, we will hear our expert, Professor Smilja Avramov. As the Defence team, we now have the same -- we are now in the same position with regards to the military expert's report. Although this expert's report, drafted by Professor Avramov, as the most eminent Yugoslav expert for international law and a person who has chaired a number of institutions, even international institutions, dealing with international law, although this report has only 15 pages, some parts of the text have been deleted from it. This deletion renders us unable to deal with some issues that the Prosecution has dealt with in the course of its case. We have analysed UN Security Council resolutions, reports by the Secretary-General of the United Nations and the General Assembly from 1991, a text about the premature recognition of Croatia and Slovenia, and all those parts have simply been deleted from our expert's report. The Prosecutor called evidence about reports filed by the ECMM, acting as a mediator in the Yugoslav crisis, and presented evidence on the basis of what their staff did on the ground in the former Yugoslavia, yet texts that pertain to the mediation of the European Union in this respect have been deleted from our report. So we believe, Your Honours, that this is, in fact, interfering with the way -- how we intend to present our case. We believe that the Trial Chamber can make a decision in this matter only after hearing both parts -- both parties. You have to hear how the international community acted in the situation. This cannot be deemed irrelevant, Your Honour, because we may have taken half of the time here in the courtroom dealing with the Vance Plan, because this shows how the international community treated the situation in the former Yugoslavia. Very important witnesses were called by the Prosecution to deal with the issue of how the international community viewed the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, yet when we try to see how the situation was dealt with when our expert wants to analyse this, then this is treated as irrelevant. This is really difficult for us to understand. An expert can, of course, have his or her view, and the Prosecution is, of course, free to agree or disagree with it; but the validity of the report will be weighed in light of all the other evidence. To say to the Defence, "You cannot use this portion" in a situation where the indictment, in its very foundation, is based inter alia on the secession of Croatia, these documents are referred to in the very counts or the very paragraphs of the indictment, and there are paragraphs in the indictment talking about the Presidency, what the Presidency did, the decisions taken by Croatia and Slovenia. We are brought in a situation, when we are treated unequally, when you compare it with the way that the Prosecution was able to present its case. Mr. Theunens spoke about the constitutional role of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Presidency, and everything else. To cut a long story short - and I don't want to now be talking about the merit of the case and to speak about the weight of the evidence - we apply to the Trial Chamber to make it possible for the Defence to examine its expert in the way that it has planned to do. To do it like this would be, in our opinion, to bring into question the right of the Defence to present its case the way it sees fit. We simply cannot see how the Prosecution, or even the Trial Chamber, can have the right to do so, in light of the circumstances that I just presented. Because this is an urgent matter, this should be dealt with by the Trial Chamber in a written or oral decision before the testimony via videolink begins tomorrow. To eliminate the topics that have been eliminated would not make the proceedings shorter and, in fact, would facilitate the understanding of the matter by the Trial Chamber. The key elements have been deleted, pertaining to the application of the Geneva Conventions. On Friday, I mentioned Protocols I and II of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and the expert deals precisely with the interpretation of secession, armed rebellion, and the attitude of the international community towards a high signatory of the Geneva Conventions. So how can we be denied the right to deal with those issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not going to be long. You just asked a question: You don't know how the Chamber has the right to do this. The Chamber has the right to do this in terms of Rule 89(C). The next point you raised which I'm going to respond to is: You're asking the Chamber, either by oral or written decision, to deal with the situation. May I request, as we did this morning, that the Defence deals with this matter by written submission, and the Chamber will deal with it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know about this order by the Trial Chamber and we really complied with it as much as we could, wherever it was possible. Now, this can all stop making any sense. Tomorrow, and perhaps the day after tomorrow, we will hear Professor Avramov via videolink, and the appeals and the -- any decision that will be made after this witness has already been heard can hardly have any effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would just note that the Trial Chamber's decision, written decision, on this issue came out on the 9th of November, last Thursday. The Defence has had several days to file a reconsideration of that order, if that was the course they wanted to take. To wait until a quarter to seven the day before the witness is to come, I think, is a little unfair. And I would say, also, I don't think the Defence has -- they had -- we filed a motion; they responded. They had an opportunity to raise all their issues. I don't think they raised anything new now which, in any way, justifies changing the Trial Chamber's thorough, well-reasoned, careful decision on this issue. I'm happy to address -- try to address those issues, if Your Honours wish, but I really think this course is not fair, and I don't think there is a basis for changing the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you want to make any submissions, by all means, go ahead, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll just touch on briefly some of the issues that were raised, and I didn't try to list all the issues. If there is any issue that gives pause to the Trial Chamber, I'm happy to give it further consideration. So this isn't necessarily exhaustive. But the first point is, the Defence has suggested now and again -- they had earlier today, that there is some unfairness, that the Prosecution got to do things a certain way and the Defence is not being allowed to do it the same way. I would reject that completely. To the extent the Prosecution solicited the views of the international community on certain issues, those were relevant and done in a proper procedural way, we would submit. They were not objected to, that is, the international community's views on issues that are relevant to this trial; for example, treatment of the Croatian -- Croat civilians in the RSK, and so forth. So the -- and they were brought -- this information was brought in through the proper witnesses. The issue with this witness is she is an expert and we objected that certain areas that she covered were not within her expertise, and the Trial Chamber also found that certain areas that she talked about were not relevant to -- either not relevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber or have been sufficiently covered both by the Prosecution, the Defence, and no further evidence was needed, I believe, on that second point. I don't recall if that was actually touched on by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, sorry to interrupt you, but what about Mr. Milovancevic's point of drawing a reference to the expert Theunens and the fact that, in his opinion, he would have been allowed to testify on some of those very issues and areas that the Prosecution objected to their expert covering? What would your response be there? Because that, for me, would be more pointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- for one thing -- I'm not sure what areas he's talking about. But, for one thing, Mr. Theunens was a different kind of expert. He was a military expert, and so he -- to the extent that he commented on military doctrine or military law, that necessarily -- would not necessarily and, in fact, would not be an area that a legal expert could comment on. Secondly, in my view, Mr. Theunens, when he commented on the law, the constitution and so forth, those were with respect to pertinent issues in the trial, that is, the command and control of the army, of the TO, and so forth. The issues that have been redacted from this expert report are not issues which are pertinent to the trial. The international community's reaction and their behaviour towards the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the mediation by the European Community is not relevant to this case. It's not relevant. So those issues -- so the issues that have been -- so it's apples and oranges, to compare -- to try, on the fly, you know, in this sort of way, to sort of draw loose comparisons between what the Prosecution experts testified about or Prosecution witnesses and what's in this report, it's really trying to compare apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do you see the dissolution of Yugoslavia itself as being relevant to the issues? If not the response of the European Community and the mediation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, certainly the dissolution of Yugoslavia is in the background of this case and there are certain issues which have arisen, for example, the right to self-determination and those issues, which have been really very thoroughly canvassed and which remain in the report. Those parts have not been redacted. That is in the report. That has been left in the report. So I'm not going to say that every issue that falls under the category of dissolution of Yugoslavia is not relevant. But what I think the Trial Chamber did is went through the report, and those issues -- those sections which were relevant to the issues in the trial have been left in and can be talked about, and those parts that are not are out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look, I think we should stick to this order that the Chamber has just made, that any objections must be made in written form and the Chamber will deal with them. Just like Mr. Milovancevic was expecting the Chamber to give either an oral or written decision now, let's get these things on paper and let's apply our minds to them and deal with them. I don't think we can give a decision between now and 7.00. On that note, the court is adjourned to tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
